title: Counting your stock with Jholok
text:
Welcome
Jholok helps a jewellery shop know what it has. It keeps a list of your products, records every piece that comes in or goes out, and helps you count what is really on the shelves, so you can see what is missing before it costs you.
This guide is for anyone using Jholok for the first time: the shop’s owner, the people who approve counts, and the staff who count. You don’t need to know anything about accounting. Each idea is explained the first time it appears, and every word is in the Glossary.

title: Counting your stock with Jholok
text:
How this guide is arranged

The ideas behind the app explains stock, the ledger and counting in plain words. Read this part first, even if you only count.
Everyday use sets the shop up and keeps the catalogue and stock up to date.
Counting walks through a count, from opening it to counting boxes of pieces.
Checking a count is for the owner and the people who approve counts.
Looking after your shop covers backups and privacy, and ends with stories from a shop’s year.

Each chapter says who it is for, starts with what you’ll learn and ends with what to remember. Words that may be new are linked to the Glossary the first time they appear.

Where to start

If you count stock, read 1  Stock basics to 3  Counting and checking against the ledger, then the chapters on counting.
If you approve counts, read those too, then the chapters on checking a count.
If you own the shop, read the guide in order.

title: Counting your stock with Jholok
text:

Every example and picture uses the same made-up shop, Jholok Jewellers, with its owner Bidisha and staff Sita, Ramesh and Meena. It is the same shop that the app’s demo shows, so what you read here matches what you see on the screen. None of its stock is real.

title: 1  Stock basics
text:
1.1 The idea
Your stock is the jewellery the shop owns and means to sell. To look after it, you need to know three things about every piece: what it is, how many of it there are, and what it’s worth. This chapter covers the first and the last. How many there are is the subject of the next two chapters.

title: 1  Stock basics
text:
Products and SKUs
Each design the shop sells is a product. A product is one design, in one metal and one weight, so that every piece of it is alike. The Temple Lakshmi jhumka in 22K gold weighing 14 g is one product. The antique jhumka in 22K weighing 8 g is another, even though both are jhumkas.
Each product has a short code called its SKU, which stands for stock keeping unit. The Temple Lakshmi jhumka’s SKU is EAR-0002. A SKU belongs to one product only. You can change it with Edit, but it is best to keep it the same, because labels and files use it. Jholok treats small and capital letters as the same, so ear-0002 is the same SKU as EAR-0002. When you add a product, Jholok suggests a SKU from its type (EAR for earrings, RIN for rings), or you can use your own codes.
How many of a product the shop holds is its stock on hand.


Types and units
Products are grouped into types: in the demo shop these are Earrings, Rings, Necklaces, Bangles, Sets, Coins and Other. A type decides the unit its products are counted in:

Earrings are counted in pairs. A pair is sold together, so it is counted together. A single earring found on its own is not half a pair, so it is never rounded into one: count the whole pairs, and add the single with Singles in the count sheet. It shows beside the pairs (“5 pairs + 1 single”), the approver sees it in Review, and it never changes stock.
Sets are counted as one. A necklace with its matching earrings is one set, and counts as 1, because it is sold as one.
Everything else is counted in pieces: a ring, a chain, a coin.

Because the units are different, Jholok keeps them apart when it says what is in stock: “30 pairs · 20 sets · 120 pieces”, not one total. Adding a pair of studs to a bridal set gives a number that means little.
Jholok never adds them into one count of items, even for sales. Where several kinds sold, it lists each, such as “18 pairs and 13 pieces”. Where a rupee value says enough, as in “Last week sold ₹7.79 L”, it gives the value alone.


Cost, list price and value
Each product can have two amounts:

its cost: what the shop paid for one, with the gold, the making charge and any stones included;
its list price: what the shop asks a customer for one (the product page calls it Price).

Stock value is what the stock is worth: each product’s stock on hand times its cost, added up. Value at cost is what the shop has paid for the stock it holds. Value at list price is what it would take if everything sold at the list price. The gap between the two is the shop’s margin.
Large amounts are written in lakh and crore, as in the app. One lakh (L) is ₹1,00,000, and one crore (Cr) is 100 lakh, or ₹1,00,00,000.

text:
1.2 In the app
The Catalogue tab lists the products, grouped by type.







Tap a product to open its page. The Temple Lakshmi jhumka has 2 pairs on hand. Its value, ₹4.12 L at cost, is 2 × ₹2,06,010. Cover says how long the stock lasts at the pace it has sold recently.







The Overview tab shows the whole shop: its stock value at cost, ₹2.73 Cr, and at list price, ₹3.16 Cr, and what is in stock, by unit.

title: 1  Stock basics
text:
1.3 Why it works this way

Stock is kept in its units so that every total means something. “20 sets” tells you something; “170 items” doesn’t.
A value always says what it is based on, and when. Value at cost and value at list price differ by the shop’s margin, and gold prices move. So Jholok writes “₹2.73 Cr at today’s cost, 9 Oct”, with its date, never just a figure.
Nothing is left out quietly. One product in the demo shop has no cost, so the Overview says “Leaves out 1 product with no cost” rather than counting it as ₹0.

title: 1  Stock basics
text:
1.4 How it works
For each product, Jholok multiplies its stock on hand by its cost (or its list price) and adds the results. Stock on hand itself isn’t stored anywhere: Jholok works it out from the ledger, as the next chapter explains. If a product’s stock has gone below zero (a mistake the next chapter also covers), it counts as none in the value, because no shelf holds minus one pendant.

title: 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum
text:
2.1 The idea
A ledger is a record of every change to the stock, oldest first. Each change is a movement. A movement says which product, when, and what kind of change it was. It also says how many: a plus number for stock coming in, a minus number for stock going out. It has a note, and the name of who entered it.
These are the kinds of movement you’ll meet first:
There are a few more, for loading the shop’s billing records and for stock that leaves the shop for a while. Later chapters explain them.
Stock on hand is the sum of all a product’s movements. It works like a bank passbook: the balance is every deposit minus every withdrawal, and nobody writes in a new balance by hand.
Here is the antique jhumka’s year. It opened with 6 pairs, 19 more were received, 1 was returned and 17 were sold. A count found one pair fewer than the ledger expected, and the approver accepted it. That leaves 8 pairs on hand. Two of them are out on jangad with Sharma Jewellers, so the product’s page shows 6 in the shop and 2 off the shelf: still the shop’s, but not on the shelf (Chapter 6).
The antique jhumka (EAR-0001) over the year: every kind of movement added together gives the stock on hand.

2.2 In the app
The Ledger tab lists every movement, newest first. At the top it sums up the last 30 days. In the demo shop that is 52 sold, 1 returned and 54 received.







To record a movement by hand, open the product and tap Receive, Sell or Adjust. The kinds are also at the top of the screen, where you choose Returned for a customer’s return. For Received, Sold or Returned, enter how many. For Adjust, enter the stock you really have and a reason. Check the date: it should be when the movement happened, which may be earlier than when you enter it. title: 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum
text:
2.3 Why it works this way
Suppose someone could simply change the antique jhumka’s stock from 8 to 7. The missing pair would vanish without a trace: nobody could tell whether it was sold, lost, or a typing slip. With a ledger, every change has a date, a kind, a note and a name. The question “where did it go?” always has an answer to look up.
So a mistake is never erased. It is put right with another movement, and both stay in the ledger. This unbroken history is called an audit trail. It lets the owner, an accountant or an insurer check the stock long after the day.
crumbs: 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum

title: 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum
text:
2.4 How it works
Jholok stores movements, never stock numbers. Whenever a screen shows stock, Jholok adds up that product’s movements up to that moment. The same sums give the stock on any past date, which is how the Overview draws its charts.

When stock goes below zero
A shelf can’t hold fewer than nothing, so stock below zero always means a movement is missing or wrong. The Lakshmi pendant (NEC-0003) sold its last piece on 26 Sep. On 4 Oct another sale was entered, from a delivery of 6 that had arrived but hadn’t been entered yet. The ledger now says −1.







Jholok doesn’t hide this or round it to zero. It marks the product Below zero, lists it under Needs attention on the Overview, and suggests what to do: record the missing delivery, or count the product.

Question. A customer returns a ring they bought yesterday. How do you record it, and what happens to the ring’s stock?






TipAnswer





Open the ring, tap Receive, choose Returned at the top, and enter 1. Its stock goes up by one. The sale stays in the ledger too, so the history shows both: sold, then returned.





Every change to stock is a movement in the ledger, with a kind, a date, a note and a name.
Stock on hand is the sum of the movements. Nobody types in a stock number.
Mistakes are put right with another movement, never erased.
Stock below zero means a movement is missing. Find it, or count the product.

title: 3  Counting and checking against the ledger
text:
3.1 The idea
The ledger says what should be in the shop. A count, sometimes called a stock take, finds what is there. For each product, Jholok puts the two numbers side by side:
Comparing them, and explaining every difference, is called reconciliation. A count can cover the whole shop or just a few types. You give it a name, such as Showcase 1, but Jholok expects every piece of those types to be counted, wherever it is in the shop.
crumbs: 3  Counting and checking against the ledger

title: 3  Counting and checking against the ledger
text:
expected: what the ledger says should be there;
counted: what the counters found.



Short and over
When the two numbers agree, the product matched. When they don’t:

short means fewer were found than expected;
over means more were found than expected.

A difference is a question, not yet an answer. These are the usual reasons:







What happened
What the count shows




A piece was stolen, lost or damaged
short


A sale wasn’t entered
short


A delivery wasn’t entered
over


A return wasn’t entered
over


A piece was put back in the wrong tray
short in one place, over in another


A counter missed a piece, or counted one twice
short or over


Something that isn’t the shop’s stock was in the tray, such as a customer’s piece in for repair

Stock that goes missing without being sold is called shrinkage. A count is how a shop finds out how much it has lost.


Counting is blind
While a count is open, counters never see the expected numbers. People find what they expect to find: a counter who knows there should be 9 chains tends to stop at 9, or to look until a ninth turns up. A counter who doesn’t know just counts. That is called a blind count.




Counting the necklaces in Showcase 2: no stock, nothing expected.





Two checks before stock changes

A shortage is counted again first. Review won’t let anyone accept a shortage until the product is recounted, and the recount is blind too: the first count and the ledger stay hidden. Many shortages on a first count are counting slips, and a recount finds them before the stock is changed.
Someone who didn’t count approves. The counter submits the count for review. Only an approver who didn’t count in it, or the owner, can open Review and complete it. They give a reason, then sign with their PIN (the owner can use Face ID). This is called separation of duties: the person who might have lost a piece isn’t the one who decides it is lost.






A count’s life. Counting stops when it’s submitted; the approver can send it back for more counting, with a reason.






What completing a count changes
Completing a count changes stock only for the differences the approver left ticked. Each one becomes a count adjustment in the ledger, so stock is still a sum of movements. Products in the count that nobody counted keep their stock, unless the approver chooses Set to zero.
Overs start unticked. An over is often a missing record (a delivery or a return nobody entered), and the right fix is to enter that record, not to make the stock up to the count.

Review puts the counted and expected numbers side by side, and lists the differences.







A shortage, or a line whose stock moved while it was being counted, waits under Recount first, with its numbers hidden until it is recounted.







When the count is completed, its Result says what was counted, what was short and over, and what changed. This is the demo’s count at Showcase 1 on 26 September.

title: 3  Counting and checking against the ledger
text:
3.3 Why it works this way

Blind counts are honest counts. Knowing the answer changes what people find.
A loss someone counted is never accepted on one count. Shortages cost the shop money, and a recount is cheap. (Products nobody counted are different: they keep their stock unless the approver chooses Set to zero.)
Two people, not one. One person can’t count a loss away and approve it too. The activity log records who counted, who approved and why.
Short and over are kept apart. If a shortage of ₹1,16,640 and an over of ₹57,780 were netted into one figure, a real loss would hide behind something that isn’t stock at all.
No percentages on small numbers. Jholok writes “3 of 4 matched” rather than 75% when fewer than 10 products were counted, because a percentage of a handful sounds more certain than it is.

title: 3  Counting and checking against the ledger
text:
3.4 How it works
At Showcase 1, the counters counted 13 products of Earrings and Rings, and 11 matched: Jholok writes that as “11 of 13 matched (85%)”. The jhumka (Antique, 22K, 8 g) was one pair short. It was recounted, still one short, and the approver accepted it: a count adjustment of −1. The hoop (Hammered, 22K, 15 mm, 4 g) was one pair over. The count’s note explains why: a customer’s repair piece was in the tray. It wasn’t the shop’s stock, so the over was left unticked and the stock didn’t change.

Question. A count finds one gold coin more than expected. What should you check before accepting it?






TipAnswer





Whether a delivery or a return of coins hasn’t been entered, and whether the coin is really the shop’s (a customer’s, say). If a record is missing, enter it and leave the over unticked: the ledger then matches the count without a count adjustment.





A count compares what the ledger expects with what is really there.
Counting is blind: counters never see the expected numbers.
A difference is a question. A shortage is recounted before it’s accepted, and an over usually means a missing record.
Someone who didn’t count approves, and only the differences they tick change the stock.

title: 4  Setting up the shop
text:
4.1 The idea
Jholok works on its own from the first launch: it already knows the usual types of jewellery and how each is counted. A few minutes of setting up makes it fit your shop:

title: 4  Setting up the shop
text:
Product types: check that the types match how your shop groups its stock.
Products: add them one by one, or import a spreadsheet (Chapter 5).
Shop details: your shop’s name and address, printed on count reports.
People: who counts and who approves, each with their own PIN.
The lock: on by default, so the app stays private.


Owner, approvers and counters
Everyone who uses Jholok has a role:

The owner runs the shop in Jholok. There is one owner, who sets up the people and proves it’s them for exports and backups.
An approver opens a count’s Review and completes it, but only for a count they didn’t count in. Approvers can count too.
A counter counts, and submits the count for review.

This is the separation of duties from Chapter 3: one person counts, another checks. The owner may approve a count they counted in only when nobody else can, and the count then says so: “Counted and approved by Bidisha (one person)”.
Each counter and approver has a PIN of 4 to 6 digits. It shows who entered each figure, and an approver’s PIN is their signature on a completed count.

title: 4  Setting up the shop
text:
4.2 In the app

Product types
Open Settings, then Product types. Each type shows how many products it has and the unit it’s counted in.








Tap + to add a type. Give it a name, choose what it’s counted in (pieces, pairs or sets), and pick a symbol.
Tap a type to rename it or change its unit. Changing the unit doesn’t convert existing stock: 4 pieces become 4 pairs. So choose the unit before adding products.
Tap Edit to drag the types into the order you like.
A type that has products can’t be deleted.



Shop details and preferences
In Settings, under Preferences:

Shop: your shop’s name and address. They head every count report. Add your GSTIN after the address if your accountant wants it on the reports.
Currency and Appearance (light, dark, or the phone’s setting).
Supplier lead time: how many days a reorder takes to arrive, 21 by default. A product whose stock won’t last that long at its recent pace of sales shows as running low (Chapter 7).










People
Open Settings, then People. Until you set People up, Jholok asks nobody who’s counting, and counts name nobody. That’s fine for trying the app out, but set it up before your first real count.

Enter your name and tap Set up People. On a phone with Face ID, Face ID proves it’s you; an owner PIN is optional, as a second way in. On a phone without Face ID, set an owner PIN.
Tap Add person for each member of staff. Enter their name, choose Counter or Approver, and let them choose their own PIN.












The demo shop's people.



A PIN must be 4 to 6 digits. Jholok refuses easy ones: one digit repeated (1111), a run (1234) and the most common PINs. After 5 wrong tries in a row, the person waits a minute before trying again, and longer after each further 5 wrong tries.
To change someone’s role or reset their PIN, tap their name. When someone leaves, Archive them: they can no longer sign in, and the log keeps their name. Nobody is ever deleted, so the history stays complete.


The activity log
At the bottom of People, Activity log lists everything that happened: every count entry, box, review, completion and movement, and every change to People, each with who and when. Nothing in it can be edited or removed.









The lock
In Settings, under Security, Require Face ID is on from the start. Jholok asks for Face ID, or the phone’s passcode, when it opens and when you come back after a minute away. You can choose how soon it locks: straight away, or after 1, 5 or 15 minutes. Whenever the app isn’t in front, a plain cover hides it from the phone’s list of open apps.
Turning the lock off asks the owner to prove it’s them.

title: 4  Setting up the shop
text:
4.3 Why it works this way

Two people, not one. Roles make sure the person who counts isn’t the person who accepts a loss.
Once People is set up, the owner proves it’s them with Face ID or the owner PIN, not the phone’s passcode (except to reset a forgotten owner PIN). On a phone shared in the shop, staff may know the passcode. Everything that takes data off the phone (exports, backups, box photos) and every change to People asks the owner each time.
Nobody is deleted, and the log can’t be edited. A shop’s records are only worth something if they can’t be quietly changed later.
The lock is on by default, because costs and stock are private, and a phone left on the counter shouldn’t show them.

title: 4  Setting up the shop
text:
4.4 How it works
PINs are never stored as typed: Jholok keeps them in a scrambled form that can’t be turned back into the PIN. Each log entry carries a code made from its own details and the code of the entry before it, so the entries form a chain. If anyone changed or removed an entry in the phone’s files, the chain would break, and the log would say so: “The log was changed after entry 12”, instead of “intact”.
If the owner forgets their PIN on a phone without Face ID, it can be reset with the phone’s passcode. The log records that, and the next count’s result says so, so a reset can’t go unnoticed.

title: 5  The catalogue
text:
5.1 The idea
The catalogue is the list of every product the shop sells (Chapter 1). Each product has a name, a type, a SKU, and optionally a variant, a barcode, a cost, a list price, a photo and notes. Jholok needs the catalogue before it can record movements or count anything.
There are two ways to build it: add products one at a time, or import them all from a spreadsheet. Most shops start with an import, then add new designs by hand as they arrive.

title: 5  The catalogue
text:
Barcodes and piece tags
Two kinds of code can be printed on a label, and they’re used differently:

A barcode belongs to a product. Every piece of the same design carries the same barcode, just like its SKU.
A piece tag belongs to one individual piece. No two pieces share a tag, even pieces of the same design. Billing software often prints one for each piece.

Because a piece tag is unique, scanning it during a count counts exactly one piece, and scanning it twice is noticed. A barcode or SKU can’t do that, so Jholok never accepts a product’s barcode or SKU as a piece tag. The tag list says which product each piece tag belongs to.

title: 5  The catalogue
text:
5.2 In the app

Add a product
In the Catalogue tab, tap +.








Photo: choose one or take one. Without a photo, Jholok draws a picture of the piece from its type and name.
Name and Type: required.
Variant: what sets this design apart, such as “Temple Lakshmi, 22K, 14 g”.
SKU: leave it blank and Jholok makes one from the type, such as EAR-0009, or type your own. No two products can share a SKU.
Barcode: the product’s barcode, if it has one.
Cost and Price: what you paid for one, and what you ask. Cost puts a value on stock and on what a count finds short or over.
Opening stock: how many the shop has now. It goes into the ledger as an opening stock movement. After that, stock changes only through movements: receipts, sales, returns, adjustments and counts.

Editing a product later never changes its stock.


A product’s page
Tap a product in the catalogue to open its page. At the top, On hand, Value and Cover (Chapter 1), or In the shop, Off the shelf and Value when some of it is sent out (Chapter 6), then a sentence about its pace of sales, the buttons to record a movement (Chapter 6), its stock history, its details and every movement.







From the ⋯ menu, Archive a product you no longer sell: it leaves the catalogue and the counts, but its history stays. A product with no history at all can be deleted instead.


Photos
Photos help people recognise products during a count. Picture matching (Chapter 9) compares box photos only with product photos, never with drawings. From the catalogue’s options menu, Take photos goes through every product without a photo, the most valuable first. For a catalogue that looks good together, use the same ivory card each time, in daylight, with the piece filling most of the frame.
Where a product has no photo, Jholok draws one. During counting, a small pencil marks a drawing, so nobody mistakes it for a photo of the piece in their hand.


Import a catalogue from a spreadsheet
Save the spreadsheet as a CSV file, then open Settings and tap Import catalogue from CSV.
The file needs a name and a type column. These are optional: sku, variant, barcode, cost, price and on_hand (the stock). Common other headings work too, such as “Product”, “Category”, “Code”, “MRP” or “Qty”. Amounts can be written as 1200, 1,200.50, ₹1,23,456, Rs. 450 or 450 INR.
Nothing changes until you’ve seen what the import will do. The preview lists the new products, the products it will update, and any rows it has to skip, with the reason and the line number, so you can fix them in the spreadsheet.


Piece tags
To link tags you already have, import a tag list: a CSV file with a tag and a sku column, such as an export from your billing software. Open Settings and tap Import tag list from CSV. The preview shows the new tags and anything it can’t use: tags already on another product, SKUs not in the catalogue, and product codes that aren’t piece tags.







To link tags one product at a time, open the product, tap Tags, then Scan to add tags, and hold each tag in front of the camera. A tag that won’t scan can be typed.

title: 5  The catalogue
text:
5.3 Why it works this way

Importing never changes the stock of a product Jholok already has. A spreadsheet is often out of date. If its stock differs, the preview says how many products differ and suggests counting them instead. While a count is open, it doesn’t compare stock at all. Stock only changes through movements (Chapter 2).
A blank cell never erases anything. If the spreadsheet has no cost for a product that has one in Jholok, the cost stays.
One SKU, one product. Jholok treats ear-0002 and EAR-0002 as the same, so a second product can’t take the code by accident.
A piece tag is one piece. That’s what lets a scan count a piece exactly once.

title: 5  The catalogue
text:
5.4 How it works
The import matches rows to products by SKU. A row with a SKU Jholok knows updates that product’s details. A row with a new SKU, or no SKU, makes a new product, and its on_hand becomes its opening stock. A type Jholok hasn’t seen becomes a new type. Jholok guesses its unit: pairs if the name has “earring” in it, sets if the name is or ends in “set” or “sets”, and pieces for the rest. You can change it in Settings → Product types.

TipAnswer

A product needs a name and a type. Jholok makes a SKU if you don’t give one.
Opening stock goes into the ledger. After that, stock changes only through movements.
Importing never changes existing stock, and a blank cell never erases a value.
A barcode belongs to a product; a piece tag belongs to one piece.

title: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out
text:
6.1 The idea
Between counts, the ledger stays right only if every movement is recorded: each delivery, each sale and each return. The billing system may record sales too; Jholok needs them as well, because its stock is the sum of its own movements (Chapter 2).
Three habits keep it right:
crumbs: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out

title: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out
text:
Record it when it happens, or as soon as you can, with the date it really happened.
Never fix a figure by guessing. If the stock is wrong, find out why. If you can’t, count the product.
Write a note when it will help someone later: the supplier, the bill number, why a piece was taken out.


Stock that leaves the shop for a while
Not all stock is on the shelf. Jewellers often send pieces out and expect them back:

Jangad: pieces sent out on approval, with a memo, for a customer or another jeweller to see.
Karigar: pieces with the craftsman, for repair or alteration.
Order: pieces set aside for a customer’s order.

These pieces are still the shop’s: they count in its stock and its value. But they aren’t on the shelf, so a count mustn’t expect them there. Jholok keeps them apart: a product shows how many are in the shop and how many are off the shelf.





Where stock can be. All of it is the shop’s; a count checks only the shop.
crumbs: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out

title: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out
text:
6.2 In the app

Receive, sell and return
Open the product and tap Receive or Sell. You can also tap + in the Ledger and choose the product, or, when no sales are recorded yet, tap Record a sale on the Overview.








Choose the kind: Received, Sold or Returned.
Set the quantity.
Add a note if it will help: the supplier, the bill number.
Check the date and time. If the movement happened earlier, set when it happened; Jholok keeps both, and the ledger shows the day it was entered too. A date can’t be in the future.
Entered by shows the owner. If someone else is entering it, tap Change, choose your name and enter your PIN. (It appears once People is set up.)
Tap Save.

Below the quantity, Jholok shows what the stock will be, unless the product is being counted. If a sale would take it below zero, it says so, but lets you save: if the sale happened, record it, then count the product to find what’s missing.


Put a stock figure right
If a product’s stock is wrong for a reason you know (a piece damaged and sent for melting, say), open it, tap Adjust, and enter the correct stock. A reason is required. Jholok records the difference as an adjustment, with your reason, in the ledger.
In the demo, a chain (Rope, 22K, 18 in, 10 g) was taken out on 22 January: “Damaged on display, sent for melting”.
Adjust is turned off for a product while a count covers it, until the count is reviewed. Use the count to put its stock right instead.


Send stock out, and bring it back
Open the product and tap Send out. An approver or the owner signs it with their PIN.








To: Jangad, Karigar or Order.
How many, or choose the pieces by their tags.
Party: who has it, and Memo: the memo number.
Due back: when it should come back. Jholok suggests 7 days for jangad and 30 for the karigar, and none for an order; change it if you agreed otherwise.

The product’s page then shows an Off the shelf section, with each memo, who has it and when it’s due. When the pieces come back, tap ⋯ beside the memo and choose Back in. If the customer keeps them, choose Sold from here. Both are signed by an approver or the owner.
A memo more than a week overdue appears under Needs attention on the Overview (Chapter 7).
crumbs: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out

title: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out
text:
6.3 Why it works this way

A movement can’t be edited or deleted. A mistake is put right with another movement, usually an Adjust with its reason, so the ledger keeps the whole story (Chapter 2).
The date is when it happened; Jholok also keeps when it was entered. A sale entered late still lands on the right day, and anyone can see it was entered late.
A sale below zero is allowed. Refusing it would leave a real sale unrecorded. Jholok records the truth and points to the missing piece.
Adjust waits while a product is being counted. Changing the ledger in the middle of a count would change what the count is checked against.
Sending out needs an approver or the owner. Stock leaving the shop is when pieces go missing, so one of them signs for it, and every memo is logged.
crumbs: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out

title: 6  Recording what comes in and goes out
text:
6.4 How it works
Each movement stores its date, its kind, its quantity and note, who entered it and when it was entered. An Adjust stores the difference between the stock before and the correct stock you entered.
Sending out is two movements that add up to nothing: the stock leaves the shop and arrives at the place. So the stock the shop owns, and its value, don’t change, while the stock in the shop goes down. Back in moves it the other way. Sold from here records a sale from that place.
If you record a movement dated before a count that has already been completed, Jholok checks whether that count already accounted for it, so it isn’t counted twice. The owner confirms the correction, and a sale needs its bill number. Chapter 12 explains this.

A movement is never edited. Put a wrong figure right with Adjust, and give the reason.
Adjust waits while the product is being counted.
Stock on jangad, with the karigar or kept for an order is still the shop’s, but a count doesn’t expect it on the shelf. An approver or the owner signs it out and back.

title: 7  Reading the Overview
text:
7.1 The idea
The Overview is the first tab: a summary of the whole shop on one screen. It answers the owner’s daily questions. What is my stock worth, and is that going up or down? Which types hold the money? What’s selling, and what isn’t? What needs doing? How did the last count go?
Every figure comes from the ledger (Chapter 2), worked out afresh when you open the app. Nothing on the Overview can be typed in.
At the top, 3M, 6M and 1Y choose how far back the charts look: 13, 26 or 52 weeks, this week included. Needs attention always looks at the last 90 days.

title: 7  Reading the Overview
text:
7.2 In the app

Stock value







The large figure is what the stock is worth at cost, ₹2.73 Cr “at today’s cost”. The sentence under it says how that changed over the period, and which type changed most: in the demo, “Down ₹15.1 L (5%) since 12 Apr, mostly Bangles (−₹12.7 L)”. The line shows the value week by week.
Below it: the value at list price, what’s in stock in each unit, and how many products there are. The small print says what the figure leaves out, such as products with no cost. It also says past values use today’s costs. So the line shows changes in stock, not in the price of gold.


By type, Needs attention, Sales, Best sellers and Last count








By type shows how the value is shared between types, and how each has moved. Tap it for a chart of each type on the same scale.
Needs attention lists products that need something done (below).
Sales shows the value sold each week at list price, after returns.
Best sellers lists the five products that sold the most by value.
Last count says how the last count went, and names the type that has gone longest without a count, once that’s over 90 days.



Needs attention

A product only just added (in the last 30 days) isn’t called low or not selling: it hasn’t had time to show its pace.


Sales







Each bar is a week, Sunday to Saturday (with the phone set to India). The last complete week is gold. The busiest week is labelled with its festival, when there was one.

title: 7  Reading the Overview
text:
7.3 Why it works this way

Values say their basis and date (“at today’s cost, 9 Oct”; “at today’s list price”), because a figure without them can mislead.
Sales are valued at today’s list price, not the price charged. Jholok doesn’t record discounts, so this shows how much stock sold, not the takings. Your billing system has the takings.
Nothing is quietly left out. The small print says how many products have no cost or price, and names the types being counted.
While a count is open, the stock of the types being counted is hidden, with a note at the top: “Stock for Necklaces is hidden while the count at Showcase 2 is open.” Sales, Best sellers and Last count stay.

title: 7  Reading the Overview
text:
7.4 How it works
The value line takes each product’s stock on each day, from the ledger, and values it at today’s cost. Archived products are left out. A product’s pace is the number it sold in the last 90 days, after returns, divided by the days it was in stock (at least 14), and its cover is how many days its stock lasts at that pace. Running low means cover shorter than the supplier lead time, which you can change in Settings → Preferences.
The sales figures are rupees at today’s list price, which can be added up. Units sold never are, because a pair, a set and a piece are different things. Under the sales bars, the Sales screen has a small panel each for pairs, sets and pieces sold, each on its own scale. Where a sentence needs a count, it lists the kinds: “Together they sold 18 pairs and 13 pieces in 90 days.” Until products have list prices, the whole Sales section works in units this way, such as “79 pairs · 17 sets · 63 pieces sold”.

title: 8  A count from start to finish
text:
8.1 The idea
Chapter 3 explained why counts matter. This chapter is the counter’s side: the steps on the phone, from starting a count to handing it over for review.
Three things are worth knowing before you start:
crumbs: 8  A count from start to finish

title: 8  A count from start to finish
text:
A count can be small. It can cover the whole shop, a few types, or the pieces in one showcase. Smaller, more frequent counts find problems sooner.
You count blind. Nothing on the counting screen shows how many there should be. While the count is open, the rest of the app hides the stock of the types being counted too.
Every tap is saved at once. If the phone rings or the app closes, the count is still there when you come back.
crumbs: 8  A count from start to finish

title: 8  A count from start to finish
text:
8.2 In the app

Start a count
In the Count tab, tap New count (the + at the top).








Location: where you’re counting, such as “Front case”. The places used in recent counts are offered below the field, so you can tap one.
What to count: leave All types on to count everything, or turn it off and tick the types you want. Each type says when it was last counted.
Notes: anything the approver should know. It’s optional.

The line under the types says how many products the count covers, and reminds you that “Expected stock stays hidden until you review, so it can’t sway the count.” Tap Start.
The Count tab also suggests what to count next: under Last counted, a button such as “Count Sets” opens a new count of the type that has gone longest without one.









Say who’s counting
If the owner has set up People (Chapter 4), the app asks Who’s counting? Choose your name if it isn’t already chosen, and enter your PIN.







You stay signed in while the count is open, even if you leave the app for up to 15 minutes. After that, or if you go back to the list of counts, the app asks again, with your name already chosen. Several people can count in one count: each signs in with their own name, and the count lists everyone who counted.


Count each product
The counting screen lists the products in the count, grouped by type. The card at the top shows how far you’ve got, such as “4 of 9 products counted”.







Each product has three controls:

+ adds one. Tap it once for each piece, pair or set as you pick it up. It sits on the right, under your thumb.
− takes one away, if you tapped once too often.
The number shows your count. A dash (–) means the product hasn’t been counted yet. Tap the number to type a count instead.

When you tap the number, choose Add to add to what you’ve counted so far (useful when you count tray by tray), or Set total to type the whole count. The sheet shows the count so far and the new total before you tap Done. For earrings, the sheet also has Singles, “An earring with no mate”: enter an odd single there, never as a pair (Chapter 1).







Two quick actions are hidden behind a swipe on a product:

Swipe right for None here, when you’ve looked and there are none. This counts 0, which is different from not counting it at all.
Swipe left for Clear, to take your count off and start again. It’s there once you’ve counted the product yourself.

A swipe only shows the button: you still have to tap it. That way a stray swipe while your other hand holds a tray never changes a count.


Put a mistake right
After any change of more than one, and after every Clear, a bar at the bottom offers Undo for a few seconds. It says what changed, such as “Chain set to 7 pieces, was 9 pieces.” Tap Undo to put the count back exactly as it was.









Find a product quickly
Type in Find a product to search by name, SKU or barcode. The filter button at the top shows only the products Not counted, or only those Counted, which helps you check nothing was missed.
To find a product from its label, tap the barcode button, Find by code. Scan or type a barcode, a SKU or a piece tag, and the list shows only that product’s row. Finding a product never counts it: you still tap +.







The buttons at the bottom, Scan tags and Box photo, count a whole tray or box at once. Chapter 9 explains them.


Submit the count
When you’ve counted everything, tap Submit (it stays greyed out until something is counted). The app checks that you mean it. If pieces in box photos are still to identify, it offers Identify now or Submit anyway (Chapter 10).







After you submit, counting stops and the count waits for an approver. Nobody can change a figure unless an approver who didn’t count in it, or the owner, taps Reopen for counting and gives a reason.

title: 8  A count from start to finish
text:
8.3 Why it works this way

One hand is enough. Counting happens with a tray in the other hand. The

is large and stays at the right edge, under the thumb, and the phone gives a small tap of feedback with every change.

No swipe changes a count by itself, for the same reason.
Nothing shows stock while you count. Not the counting screen, and not the rest of the app either: the Catalogue shows “Being counted” for the types in an open count, and the Overview leaves them out, with a note at the top.





The Overview while the necklaces are being counted.




None here is not the same as not counted. “None here” says you looked and found nothing. A product left with a dash wasn’t counted, and keeps its stock unless the approver decides otherwise.
Submitting stops counting so that the approver reviews a count that can’t change under them.

title: 8  A count from start to finish
text:
8.4 How it works
Your count is saved with every tap, together with who entered it and when. The activity log records each figure, so if several people count, it’s clear who counted what. Pieces counted from box photos or tag scans add to the same number as your taps; Chapter 9 explains how the two are kept apart.
When you submit, the count waits under In progress in the Count tab, marked “Waiting for approval”. An approver then reviews it, as Chapter 3 explained.

title: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos
text:
9.1 The idea
Counting a box of 15 pairs one tap at a time works, but it’s slow. Jholok can count a whole box at once, in one of two ways:
A box holds many designs of one type, each pair or set on its own card or in its own slot. So the app counts cards, not loose pieces: one card is one pair, or one set.
Either way, the result is a proposal. The review says “15 pairs proposed”: nothing reaches the count until you’ve checked it and tapped Add.
The app counts cards. Where a card may hold two, or cards touch, it asks you; it never splits a piece on its own.
crumbs: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos

title: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos
text:
Scan tags. If each piece carries its own piece tag (Chapter 5), move the camera over the box. Each tag read counts its piece, once. This is the most reliable way, which is why Scan tags is the gold button.
Box photo. Photograph the box. Jholok finds the box, straightens it, finds each card, reads any tags it can see, and suggests a product for the rest from their pictures.









ImportantHow well box photos work hasn’t been measured yet



The app’s photo counting was built and tuned on drawn example boxes, like the ones in this guide, not on photos of real boxes. How often it gets a real shop’s boxes right isn’t known yet. That’s why every box is checked before it’s added, and why the app never adds a box by itself.
crumbs: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos

title: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos
text:
9.2 In the app
On the counting screen, the two buttons at the bottom open the camera: Scan tags and Box photo. The camera button beside each type’s name photographs a box of that type.








Scan tags

Tap Scan tags, and move the camera slowly over the tags. It reads several at once.
Each tag read joins the list with what happened to it. The phone gives a different buzz when a tag is read again, so you know to move on.
For a tag the camera can’t read, tap Type a tag and type its code. It counts once, like a scanned tag.
Tap Done to see the summary.








You see
It means




+1

This piece was counted earlier in the count, so it adds nothing


Not in your tag list
The tag isn’t linked to a product yet


Product code
A barcode or SKU, which is on every piece of a design, so it can’t count one


Not in this count

Link or skip the unknown tag, then tap Add … pairs to count: in this scan, 13 if you link it, 12 if you skip it. The scan is kept as “Tag scan 1”, and each counted tag adds one to its product.


Take a box photo

Tap Box photo. If the count covers several types, choose the box’s type at the top.
Hold the phone flat above the box, with the whole box in the frame. If it’s tilted, the app says “Hold the phone flat”. Tags it can read are ticked as you frame.
Tap the shutter. The app checks the photo, and if it’s blurred, too dark, too bright or tilted, offers Retake or Use anyway.
It then finds the pieces, reads the tags and matches pictures, and opens the box’s review.

You can also Choose photo to use one you took earlier.


Check the box
The review shows the photo with every piece outlined and numbered. A small mark on each outline says how its product was found:

a tag: read from its tag;
sparkles: suggested by its picture, waiting for you to check it;
a question mark: still needs a product;
no mark: confirmed.

A dashed outline is a piece left out, and a red ! is a piece that may be two, or was found only by its tag.

Tap any piece to open it. The sheet shows its tag, its product, and the products it may be, with a search at the top. From there:

choose the product, or accept the suggested one;
Make it 2, on a piece marked with a red ! as maybe two. If one outline holds two pieces and isn’t marked, use Add piece;

If the app missed a piece, tap Add piece, then tap where it is. For a tray with one piece per slot, such as rings, turn on Count by tray grid, set the rows and columns, and drag the corners to fit the tray.

If the box was counted already
If a box photo shares half or more of its tags with a box already added, or an untagged box looks just like one already added, the app asks first: “Is this Box 2 again?” If it is, tap Cancel, or its pieces would be counted twice.


After adding
The count lists the box under Boxes, and its pieces add to each product’s count, together with anything counted by hand. Tap a box to open its review again and update it, or swipe it to Remove it: its pieces come off the count, and its photo is deleted.

title: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos
text:
9.3 Why it works this way

Tags first. A piece tag names one piece exactly, so scanning can’t mistake one design for another.
A tag counts once per count. Whether it’s scanned twice, or appears in a photo and a scan, the piece is counted once.
Cards, not loose pieces, and never a guessed split. Earrings lie close together and sets are large; guessing would be wrong too often. Where one outline may hold two, the app asks; where pieces touch, it warns.
A proposal, never automatic. The app can’t yet show it counts real boxes well, so a person checks every box. Settings → Photo counting keeps score.
Not a piece is kept, left out. What the app got wrong is exactly what a better version needs to learn from, so the outline stays with the box, marked, and is never counted.
Picture matching never looks at stock. It compares the piece’s picture with product photos of the box’s type only.
crumbs: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos

title: 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos
text:
9.4 How it works
Every added box keeps its photo, the straightened box, and every piece you confirmed. These are kept so that, in future, the app can learn from your real boxes. The owner can export them from Settings → Export → Box photos and labels, which asks the owner to confirm each time.
Settings → Photo counting compares the app’s count of each box with the count you added after checking it. Those numbers lean towards the app, because you saw its proposal first, so they aren’t an independent measure.

title: 10  Pieces to identify later
text:
10.1 The idea
When a box’s pieces carry tags, Jholok knows each piece’s product from its tag (Chapter 9). In a box with no tags, a photo can still find the cards and count them, but it doesn’t know which design is on each card. Someone has to say.
Doing that piece by piece in the box review is slow: often slower than counting by hand. So Jholok lets you add the box first and identify its pieces later, from one list, the To identify queue.
Until a piece is identified, it counts in the box but in no product. The box adds “15 pairs”, but no product’s count goes up for that piece yet. And the count can’t be completed until every piece is identified, or marked as not in the catalogue. That way, no product is ever called short just because nobody said which pieces were its.

title: 10  Pieces to identify later
text:
10.2 In the app

Add the box
In the review of an untagged box, every piece without a product is marked for identifying later. The gold button still adds the box, and the note under it says how many pieces are left: here, all 15.




The box is a drawn example the app uses for practice, not a photo of a real shop's box.



Tap Add 15 pairs to count. The count now shows a To identify row at the top, and the type’s heading says how many of its pieces are waiting.









Identify each piece
Tap the To identify row. The queue shows one piece at a time.




The box is a drawn example the app uses for practice, not a photo of a real shop's box.




At the top: the piece’s picture, how many are left (“1 of 15” means 15 still to identify), and which box and piece it is. See the box shows the whole photo with this piece outlined, so you can find it in the tray.
Below: a search field, then picture matches (the products whose photos the piece looks most like), then every product of the box’s type, as pictures. Picture matching compares with product photos only, so products need photos for it to help.
Tap the product the piece is. The queue moves to the next piece.
Skip leaves a piece for later. When the rest are done, the queue says how many you skipped; tap Start again to go back to them.
Not in the catalogue, at the bottom, is for a design the shop has no product for. The piece is left out of the count, and the count’s result and report list it by box and piece number, so someone can add the product and count it later.

After you pick a product, if other pieces in the same box look the same, the queue offers them too, ticked: “These 3 in Box 1 look the same. Untick any that aren’t.” Untick any that differ, then tap Identify 4 as …, or Just piece 1 to identify only the first. Nothing is identified by its look alone: you always confirm.


Submit with pieces left
You can submit a count with pieces still to identify. The app offers Identify now first, and Submit anyway second, and says the count can’t be completed until they’re done. The approver’s Review then says how many pieces aren’t identified, and Complete stays off until they are. The approver reopens the count, with a reason, and a counter identifies them.

title: 10  Pieces to identify later
text:
10.3 Why it works this way

It’s quicker. One list for every box, one tap per piece, and lookalikes in one go, instead of opening each piece in each box.
Unidentified isn’t missing. A piece nobody has identified still counts in its box. Completing the count with it would call its product short, so completing waits.
Only counters identify, while counting. The approver can see what’s short. If the approver could say which product a piece was, a loss could be covered up by “finding” the missing product in a box. So the approver reopens the count, and a counter, who can’t see stock, identifies the pieces.
The queue is blind. It shows pieces and products, never stock.
A design not in the catalogue doesn’t block the count forever. It’s left out, and listed, so it gets dealt with.

title: 10  Pieces to identify later
text:
10.4 How it works
Each identification is saved at once, with who made it and when, in the activity log. The piece’s product is set, and that product’s count goes up. Identified pieces also help picture matching: until the app is closed, a piece like it in another photo is suggested that product.
Lookalikes are found by comparing the pieces’ pictures with each other, never with the stock. This needs a real phone: on the test phones used for this guide’s screenshots, the queue never offers lookalikes.
Like everything about box photos, picture matching was tuned on drawn example boxes. How well it does on a real shop’s boxes hasn’t been measured yet: always check the product before you tap it.

title: 11  Book stock
text:
11.1 The idea
Most jewellers’ billing software keeps its own list of every tagged piece in stock: the books. When a piece is billed, it drops off that list. Jholok’s ledger should agree, but a sale billed and not entered in Jholok, or a piece sent out and not recorded, makes them differ.
A count can be loaded with the books: you give Jholok the billing system’s list of tags in stock, and the time it was taken from. For the tagged products in the count, Jholok then expects what the books say, not what its own ledger says. Products with no tags keep Jholok’s own ledger. The count checks the stock against the system that bills the customers.
Because each tag names one piece, the books also make a count precise. When every piece of a product had its tag read, Jholok can name the exact tags the books have and the count didn’t find.

title: 11  Book stock
text:
The file
The billing system’s export, saved as a CSV file, with:

a tag column (also “Tag No”, “tag code” or “barcode tag”),
a SKU column (also “Item Code”, “design” or “design code”),
and optionally a status column (also “location” or “state”), saying where each piece is.

A blank status means the piece is on the shelf. Jholok knows the usual words for the other places: “jangad” or “approval”, “karigar” or “artisan”, “order” or “booked”, and “sold”. A word it doesn’t know, it asks the owner about, once, and remembers.

title: 11  Book stock
text:
11.2 In the app

Load the books
On the counting screen, tap Load book stock. An approver or the owner signs in, then chooses the file.
Set As of to the time the file was taken from the billing system. Jholok suggests the time the file was saved.
Before anything changes, the sheet shows a plan:

how many tags the file has;
for the count’s types, the new tags it will link;
the pieces it will mark sold;
the pieces off the shelf, and where;
customers’ pieces;
products with no tags, which keep Jholok’s ledger. Rows it can’t use are listed under Skipped, with the reason.








If the file uses a status word Jholok doesn’t know, the plan asks: “This file says”rep” for 14 rows. What does it mean?” The owner chooses one of On the shelf, Sold, Jangad, Karigar, Order or Customer’s piece, and taps Use this meaning. Jholok remembers the answer for every later file. The owner can change answers in Settings → Book stock words.
Tap Load. The counting screen then shows when the books are from.







From the ⋯ beside it, Load newer book stock loads a later file, and Undo book load takes the latest load back while the count is open.


When the owner is needed
Three things need the owner, even when an approver is loading:

Saying what a new status word means. Load stays off until every word has an answer.
Marking pieces sold. A tag Jholok had in stock that isn’t in the file is marked sold, which takes it out of stock.
A file that doesn’t look like the stock. The plan says so if loading would leave more than a tenth of the count’s tagged products with none. It also says so if more than one row in twenty matches nothing in the catalogue. Only the owner can Load anyway.



Before Review
If counting went on more than half an hour after the time the books are from, opening Review warns: “The books are older than the counting.” Pieces sold in between would look missing. Load newer books, or give a reason and Review anyway.

title: 11  Book stock
text:
11.3 Why it works this way

The books are the shop’s own record. Checking the stock against the billing system finds sales that never reached Jholok, and pieces that left the shop without a bill.
The “as of” time matters. A piece sold after the file was taken isn’t missing; Jholok needs the time to tell the difference.
Nobody counting sees a quantity. The plan shows tags and row counts, never a product’s stock, so loading the books doesn’t spoil a blind count.
Marking sold, and odd files, need the owner, because both can take a lot of stock off Jholok’s ledger at once.
Customers’ pieces are never stock. A piece in for repair may sit in the same tray; the books mark it, and Jholok never counts it.

title: 11  Book stock
text:
11.4 How it works
Loading is one change, saved at once:

For each tagged product in the count, and each place, Jholok records a Book stock movement: the books minus its own stock at the “as of” time. Stock is still a sum of movements, and now matches the books.
Tags in the file that Jholok didn’t know are linked to their products by SKU. A tag Jholok already knows keeps its product.
Each tag’s state is set: on the shelf, sold, or out at its place.
The load is kept with a fingerprint of the file (its SHA-256), and logged.

The count’s first load sets the starting point. A later load during the count can show pieces sold during the count: on the shelf in the first file, gone from the later one.

What the count finds about each tag
When the count is completed, Jholok freezes what it found for each product, and Result, the report and the CSV list:

Tags not found: in the books, not read in the count. These are named only for products where every counted piece had its tag read, so a missing tag really is missing. A product counted by hand says its tags weren’t checked.
Sold during the count: dropped by a later load.
Found, not in the books: read in the count, but the books don’t have them in stock.
Out of the shop: read in the count, but recorded as out, on jangad, say.

title: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off
text:
12.1 The idea
A count compares the shelf with the ledger at one moment. Two things make that moment hard to pin down in a real shop: some stock is away, and the shop stays open while it’s counted.
crumbs: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off

title: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off
text:
Stock that is away
Pieces on jangad, with the karigar, or kept for an order are the shop’s stock, but they aren’t on the shelf (Chapter 6). A count expects only what’s in the shop: owned stock minus what’s away. The rest is listed apart, so nobody mistakes it for a loss.
Customers’ own pieces, in for repair, are never the shop’s stock, wherever they sit.


The cut-off
A count takes time. If a pair of jhumkas is sold at 9:30, and the jhumkas were counted between 9:05 and 9:40, which stock should the count be compared with: before the sale, or after?
Jholok works out a cut-off for every product in a count. It reads the activity log to find when that product was counted (its counting window), and compares the count with the stock in the shop at the end of that window. If stock moved during the window, it checks every stock figure along the way: if the count matches any of them, the count is fine. If it matches none, the product needs a recount.





A sale during the counting window. A count that matches the stock before or after the sale is fine; one that matches neither is recounted.




So the shop never has to close for a count, and a sale in the middle of counting is never called a loss.
crumbs: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off

title: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off
text:
12.2 In the app

Stock off the shelf in Review
When stock in the count’s types is away, Review’s summary says so, such as “Off the shelf, not counted: 1 with the karigar”. Under the product, it says how many were away when it was counted, “not expected on the shelf”.







If a count finds more than expected while some are away, Review asks “did some come back?” and offers Back in, so a piece that came back without being recorded can be put right in the count.
After the count is completed, its Result and report list what was off the shelf when each product was counted.


Lines whose stock moved
Under a product counted before the counting ended, or recounted, Review says what its expected stock was taken from, such as “Expected as of 11:42, when it was counted”. A product whose count matches none of the stock figures during its window shows “Stock moved while counted”, and waits under Recount first with its numbers hidden, like a shortage (Chapter 13). After the recount, the recount’s own time becomes the cut-off.


Entries made after a count
Sometimes a sale is entered late, after the count that covered it was completed, but dated before the product was counted. If that count had already written the piece off as short, the shop would lose it twice: once in the count, and again in the sale.
Jholok spots this when you record the movement. The sheet says, for example: “This sale is dated before Showcase 2 counted Jhumka, which wrote 1 off as short. Jholok will put 1 back so it isn’t taken off twice.” For a sale, it asks for the bill number. Putting the piece back needs the owner, who confirms with Face ID or the owner PIN. The correction is a cut-off correction movement, logged with the sale.
If the owner doesn’t confirm, the sale can still be saved without the correction; the count then lists it as entered after completion, and its write-off stays.
The count’s Result and report list every entry made after completion, and the next Review of those types lists the corrections, so nothing changes a past count quietly.
crumbs: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off

title: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off
text:
12.3 Why it works this way

What’s away isn’t lost. Counting it as short would write off stock the shop still owns.
A shop doesn’t close for a count. The cut-off lets sales carry on during counting without spoiling it.
A late sale shouldn’t count twice. The cut-off correction puts back what the count took off, and only for that sale.
The owner decides corrections. Changing what a completed count did is serious, so it needs the owner’s proof, and it’s logged and listed.
crumbs: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off

title: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off
text:
12.4 How it works
For each product, the counting window runs from the first to the last time its count changed, as the activity log records. Expected stock is the stock in the shop at the window’s end. If movements fell inside the window, Jholok compares the count with the stock before each one and after it.
When every counted piece of a product had its tag read and the count has the books (Chapter 11), expected comes from the tags themselves: the pieces the books have on the shelf.
Completing a count freezes, for each product, its cut-off, how it was decided and how much was off the shelf. Later movements never change what the count compared.
crumbs: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off

title: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off
text:
12.5 Try it
In the screenshot above, a chain (Rope, 22K, 18 in, 10 g) went to Ramesh karigar on 24 Aug, memo K-17. When the chains were counted at Showcase 2, the shop owned 9 but had 8 on the shelf. The counter counted 9, so Review shows it 1 over, with “1 with the karigar, not expected on the shelf”.
One over, with one away: the likeliest story is that the chain came back from the karigar and nobody recorded it. Tapping Back in records it as back from when it was counted, and the line then matches.
Question. At 9:15 you count 6 pairs of hoops. At 9:20 a pair is sold. You finish the earrings at 9:40. Is the hoops’ count short?






TipAnswer





No. The hoops were counted at 9:15, before the sale, when the shop had 6. Their cut-off is 9:15, and your count matches the stock then. Had you counted 5, they would be one short: at 9:15 the sale hadn’t happened yet.





A count expects what’s in the shop. Stock on jangad, with the karigar or kept for an order is listed apart, never as a loss.
Each product’s cut-off is when it was counted. Sales during counting are fine if the count matches the stock at some point.
A product whose stock moved and matches nothing is recounted.
A movement entered late, dated before a completed count, gets a cut-off correction that the owner confirms.
crumbs: 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off

title: 13  Submit, review and complete
text:
13.1 The idea
When the counters submit a count, it waits for an approver. The approver’s job is to look at what was found, check anything doubtful, and decide which differences become changes to the stock. Until the count is completed, nothing has changed.
Review is where the expected numbers appear for the first time, so only an approver or the owner who didn’t count in it may open it (Chapter 4). The owner may approve a count they counted in only when nobody else can. It starts with safe choices already made:
The approver can change the ticks, but can’t accept a shortage that hasn’t been recounted. These rules are built into the app, not just the screen.

title: 13  Submit, review and complete
text:
A shortage must be recounted before it can be accepted. Its numbers stay hidden until then, and the recount is blind.
Overs start unticked. An over usually means a missing record: enter that instead.
A product whose stock moved during counting and matches nothing must be recounted too (Chapter 12).
Products nobody counted keep their stock, unless the approver chooses Set to zero.

title: 13  Submit, review and complete
text:
13.2 In the app

Open Review
Open the submitted count from the Count tab and tap Review. The app asks for an approver’s PIN. Only people who may approve are offered; those who counted are named as unable to.







If the count was loaded with the books, and counting went on more than half an hour after the time they’re from, the app warns first (Chapter 11).


Read Review
The card at the top says what was counted and how it compares:

how many products were counted, and in what units;
how many were short and over, in units and at cost;
a sentence: how many matched, what happens to those not counted, and how this count compares with the last count of the same types.








Below it come the sections:

Not identified: box photo pieces nobody has identified. The count can’t be completed until a counter identifies them (Chapter 10).
Recount first: shortages, and products whose stock moved, with their numbers hidden.
Discrepancies: every other difference, each with its tick, the ledger and counted numbers, and the value at cost. The line at the end says what completing would change, such as “Net if completed: −₹1.29 L at cost.”
Not counted: products in the count that nobody counted, with the choice Keep their stock or Set to zero.
Matched: folded away.










Recount
Tap a product under Recount first to recount it. The recount is blind: the first count and the ledger stay hidden until you tap Done. The app keeps the first count and when the recount happened, even if the recount confirms it.














You can recount any line under Discrepancies or Not counted by tapping it.


Choose, then complete
Tick the differences to accept. A ticked line sets stock to the count; an unticked one leaves the stock as it is. Then tap Complete count, or Complete and adjust 3 when three lines will change.







The sheet says what will change, and what won’t. Give a reason: it goes on the count and on every adjustment it writes, as “Stock count · Showcase 1 · your reason”. Recent reasons are offered to tap. Then Sign with PIN and complete.
If the count needs more counting, close Review and tap Reopen for counting on the count, with a reason. The log records that anything counted after Review was counted after it.

title: 13  Submit, review and complete
text:
13.3 Why it works this way

A second person decides. The approver didn’t count (unless the owner is the only one who can approve, and the count then says so), so a loss can’t be counted away and approved by the same person.
A loss someone counted is never accepted on one count. The recount is cheap; a wrong write-off isn’t.
Hidden until recounted. A recount that can see the ledger tends to find the ledger’s number.
The reason is written on every adjustment, so the ledger says why each change happened.
The PIN is a signature. The count records who approved it, and the log can’t be edited afterwards.
Comparisons are honest. Review says a match rate rose or fell only when the change is bigger than chance would give, with at least 10 products on each side. Otherwise it says “Too few products to call that a change.”

title: 13  Submit, review and complete
text:
13.4 How it works
Completing is one change, saved at once: if anything fails, nothing changes and the count stays open. Jholok freezes every line’s expected and counted numbers, cost, cut-off and stock off the shelf, so the count reads the same forever. For each ticked line it writes a count adjustment movement for the difference, signed by the approver, with the reason. It records who approved, when and why, and logs the completion.
A completed count can’t be edited. Mistakes found later are put right with new movements, or a new count.

The demo’s open count, at Showcase 2, covers the necklaces. Its Review card would say: counted 4 of 9 products · 19 pieces; 4 of 4 matched; 5 not counted keep their stock. The last count of the necklaces was the whole shop count on 14 Apr: 9 of 9. Both are every product matched, so Review says “The same share as then.”
At the earlier count at Showcase 1, the approver recounted the short jhumka, found it still short, and ticked it. The hoops that were over, because of a customer’s repair piece, stayed unticked. The counter had also found one single jhumka earring: Review showed it beside the pairs, as “+ 1 single”, and it changed no stock. Completing wrote one count adjustment:

title: 14  Results and the count report
text:
14.1 The idea
Once a count is completed, it becomes a record: what was counted, what was found, what changed, who counted and who approved, and why. That record can’t be edited. Jholok shows it on screen as the count’s Result, and can print it as a count report, a PDF to keep with the shop’s accounts or show an auditor or insurer.
crumbs: 14  Results and the count report

title: 14  Results and the count report
crumbs: 14  Results and the count report

title: 14  Results and the count report
text:
14.3 What’s in the report
The report is printed in black and white, on A4, so it copies and files well.




Page 1: the shop, the count, the sign-off, totals, discrepancies.




The first page: the shop’s name and address; the count’s place, types and times; what expected stock came from; the sign-off (who started, counted, submitted, reviewed and approved, and the reason); the log’s code; totals by type; and the discrepancies, each with how it was counted.





Every line, by type, with how each was counted.




Every line of the count, grouped by type.
Where they apply: the tags, what was off the shelf, customers’ pieces, pieces not in the catalogue, and entries made after completion.





A page for each box photo, its pieces numbered.




A page for each box photo, with its pieces numbered and a table of what each was and how it was identified, and each tag scan’s tags.

Every page carries the report’s fingerprint at the bottom: a code made from everything in the report. Printing it again gives the same code, unless a product was renamed, the shop’s name or address changed, or entries were made after the count was completed; then the report says so. Making a report is logged, with its fingerprint.
The report gives quantities, not rupee values.

title: 14  Results and the count report
text:
14.4 Why it works this way

A completed count is a record, not a draft. Its counts and numbers can’t be edited, so a report printed next year shows the same count.
The fingerprint shows the paper is genuine. Print the report again from the app and compare the codes: if the paper was altered, they won’t match. (A renamed product or a late entry also changes the code, and the new report says so.)
Exports ask the owner every time, because a report shows the shop’s stock, and once a file leaves the phone, Jholok can’t take it back.
Accuracy is shown honestly. No percentage on fewer than 10 products, and no “better” or “worse” unless the difference is bigger than chance.

14.5 How it works
Completing a count freezes its counts and numbers. Product names and SKUs are printed as they are on the day (the report says so), and entries made after completion are added. The fingerprint is a code worked out from everything in the report except the time it was printed. The log’s code on the report is the code of the count’s log as it was at completion: if anyone altered the log, the report would say so.
