title: 15  Keeping your data safe
text:
15.1 The idea
Jholok keeps everything on the phone: the catalogue, every movement, every count, the activity log, product photos and box photos. Nothing is sent to a server or synced to the cloud. That keeps the shop’s stock and costs private, but it means the phone holds the only copy until you make a backup.
A backup is one file with everything in it. Saved somewhere other than the phone (iCloud Drive, a computer), it lets you get the shop back if the phone is lost, broken or replaced.
Jholok doesn’t back up by itself. Make it a habit: after every completed count, and at least once a week.

title: 15  Keeping your data safe
text:
15.2 In the app

Back up
Open Settings, then Backup.




Backup, in the demo shop, where backups are turned off.



The top says when you last backed up, and some of what’s been added since (“Since then: 1 count completed and 14 box photos added”). A lost phone would lose those, and every sale, receipt and other entry made since too. A backup holds lists what goes in: products, counts, any count in progress, and box photos.

Tap Back up now.
Confirm it’s you, with Face ID or the owner PIN (until People is set up, Face ID or the phone’s passcode).
Choose where to save the file, such as iCloud Drive in the Files list, or a folder that a computer collects. The file is called something like “Jholok backup 2026-10-09 1730.jholokbackup”.

The backup holds every product and photo, every count and movement, the activity log, the box photos, and the preferences (currency, appearance, lead time, book stock words and so on).
After a count is completed, its Result reminds you if it isn’t backed up yet: “This count is only on this phone until it’s backed up.” (Chapter 14)


Restore, or move to a new phone
To restore, open Settings → Backup, tap Restore from a backup…, confirm it’s you, and choose the backup file.
Before anything changes, Jholok shows the phone and the backup side by side: when the backup was made, and how many products, counts, counts in progress and box photos each has. It warns that everything on the phone will be replaced. If the phone has data, Back up this phone first saves it before you go on. Then tap Replace with backup.
To move to a new phone, back up on the old one, install Jholok on the new one, and restore the backup there. The lock setting and the shop’s name and address (Settings → Shop) aren’t in the backup: set them again on the new phone (Chapter 4).


Privacy

The lock: Jholok asks for Face ID or the phone’s passcode when it opens and, by default, after a minute away; Settings → Security changes it (Chapter 4).
The cover: whenever Jholok isn’t in front, a plain cover hides it from the list of open apps.
The owner, every time: every export, backup, restore, report and box photo export asks the owner to confirm, with Face ID or the owner PIN (or the phone’s passcode, until People is set up).
Nothing left behind: files made for sharing are deleted as soon as the share sheet closes, and any left over are deleted when Jholok opens.



Box photos and space
Box photos take space. Settings → Photo counting → Storage says how much, and can remove photos of counts completed over 12 months ago. Each box’s pieces and numbers stay; only the photos go.

title: 15  Keeping your data safe
text:
15.3 Why it works this way

On the phone, not in the cloud, so the shop’s stock and costs are seen only by the people who hold the phone.
One file, so a backup is easy to save, copy and keep.
Side by side before restoring, so nobody replaces new data with an old backup by mistake.
The log remembers restores. After a restore, the log records it and where the log it replaced had got to. Going back to an older backup always shows.
Exports ask every time, because once a file leaves the phone, Jholok can’t take it back.

title: 15  Keeping your data safe
text:
15.4 How it works

Saving never fails silently
Every change is saved at once. If a save fails (most often because the phone is nearly full), Jholok puts everything back as it was, so the screen matches what’s stored, and says so: “The send out wasn’t saved, so it’s back as it was. If the phone is nearly full, free some space and try again.” A count whose completion fails stays open, with no stock changed.


If Jholok can’t open its data
If the data can’t be opened (after a failed update, say), Jholok doesn’t stop. It shows “Jholok can’t open its data”, and says nothing has been deleted. You can Try again, Restore from a backup…, or Save the data file…, which saves the raw data so it can be repaired. That file isn’t a backup and can’t be restored.


Restoring safely
Jholok first copies the backup next to your data, checks it and brings it up to date with the app. Only then does it replace your data. If the phone switched off part way, Jholok finishes the job the next time it opens. A backup made by an older version of Jholok is brought up to date as it’s restored. One made by a newer version can’t be restored until you update the app.


Diagnostics
Settings → Diagnostics, under About, keeps reports of crashes and hangs from iOS, and a log of what went wrong in the app, such as a failed save or a camera that stopped. It never records stock, products, prices or tags. Nothing leaves the phone unless the owner taps Share diagnostics, which makes one file to send to whoever supports the app.

title: 15  Keeping your data safe
text:
15.5 Try it
Question. The shop’s phone is stolen. What do you need to get the shop back, and what would be lost?






TipAnswer





The latest backup file, saved off the phone. Install Jholok on a new phone and restore it. Everything entered since that backup would be lost: the counts, products and box photos in the Backup screen’s “Since then” line, and every sale, receipt and other entry too. That’s why it’s worth backing up after every count.





The phone holds the only copy until you back up. Jholok doesn’t back up by itself.
Back up after every completed count, and at least weekly, to iCloud Drive or a computer.
Restoring shows the phone and the backup side by side first, and replaces everything.
Every export and backup asks the owner, and shared files are deleted afterwards.

title: 16  Stories from the shop
text:
16.3 The pendant below zero
The Overview showed one product Below zero: the Lakshmi pendant, at −1. Its last movement was a sale on 4 Oct, with the note “Walk-in, receipt of 6 not yet entered”.
The pendant had sold out, a delivery of 6 had arrived, and a customer bought one before anyone entered the delivery. Bidisha opened the pendant and tapped Receive, entered 6, and set the date to the day the delivery came. The stock became 5, and the warning went away (Chapter 6).
The lesson: below zero always means a missing movement. Find it, enter it with its real date, and the stock is right again.

title: 16  Stories from the shop
text:
16.4 The customer’s repair piece
At the count at Showcase 1 on 26 September, the hammered hoops came out one pair over. Sita, approving, didn’t accept it straight away: an over usually means a missing record. Ramesh, who led the count, told her why: a customer’s repair piece had been left in the tray.
The extra pair wasn’t the shop’s stock at all, so Sita left the line unticked. The hoops’ stock didn’t change, and the Result lists the line under Left unchanged (Chapter 14).
The lesson: keep customers’ pieces out of the trays, or mark them, and never make stock up to a count without asking why.

title: 16  Stories from the shop
text:
16.5 The karigar’s chain
A chain (Rope, 22K, 18 in, 10 g) had gone to Ramesh karigar for repair, memo K-17, due back in 30 days. By then it was 14 days late, and the Overview’s Needs attention listed it: “1 memo more than a week overdue” (Chapter 6).
Bidisha called the karigar. The chain had come back the week before and was already in the showcase, but nobody had recorded it. Sita opened the chain, tapped ⋯ beside the memo under Off the shelf, chose Back in, set Back on to the day it came back, and signed with her PIN. The chain was in the shop again, and the next count expected it on the shelf (Chapter 12).
The lesson: record pieces back in when they come back. Otherwise the next count finds them “over”, and the overdue list keeps nagging.

title: 16  Stories from the shop
text:
16.6 A new member of staff
When a new assistant joined, Bidisha added them in Settings → People as a Counter, and let them choose their own PIN (Chapter 4). Their first count was a small one, the rings in one showcase, with Ramesh beside them to show how + and the number pad work, and how − and Undo put a slip right.
Counting is blind, so the ledger couldn’t sway the new counter. And a counter can never approve a count. The activity log shows each figure they entered.
The lesson: start new staff on small counts. The app’s rules protect the shop and them: nobody can be blamed for a figure someone else entered.


Count the whole shop once to set a baseline; then count often, a few types at a time.
Record every movement when it happens, with its real date.
A difference is a question: below zero, over and short each have a usual cause worth finding.
Record pieces back in when they come back from jangad or the karigar.

title: Glossary
text:
For everyone

The words this guide uses, in plain terms, with the chapter that explains each one.

Adjustment

A movement that corrects stock outside a count, with a reason, such as a piece damaged and sent for melting. See 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum.

Approver

A person who can open a count’s Review and complete it, but only for a count they didn’t count in. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Audit trail

The unbroken record of every change to the stock: what changed, when, why and who entered it. Mistakes are corrected with new entries, never erased. See 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum.

Below zero

Stock the ledger says is less than none. It always means a movement is missing or wrong, such as a sale entered before its delivery. See 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum.

Blind count

A count in which the counters never see what the ledger expects, so they count what is there rather than what should be. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Book stock, the books

The shop’s billing system’s own record of what is in stock. Jholok can load it into a count. See 11  Book stock.

Box photo

A photo of a box of cards, from which Jholok proposes how many of each product are in it. See 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos.

Card

The small card each pair of earrings or each set sits on in a box. Jholok’s box photos count cards, not loose pieces. See 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos.

Cost

What the shop paid for one piece of a product, with the metal, the making charge and any stones. See 1  Stock basics.

Count

Finding what is really in the shop and comparing it with what the ledger expects. Also called a stock take. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Count adjustment

The movement Jholok records when an approver completes a count and accepts a difference. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Counter

A person who counts. Counters count blind, and submit the count for review. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Counting window

The time from when a product was first counted in a count to when its count last changed. Its cut-off is the end of it. See 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off.

Cover

How long a product’s stock lasts at the pace it has sold recently. See 1  Stock basics.

Crore (Cr)

One hundred lakh: ₹1,00,00,000. See 1  Stock basics.

Cut-off

The moment a count line’s expected stock is taken from, so that sales during a count don’t look like losses. See 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off.

Cut-off correction

A movement that puts back what a completed count took off, when a sale, delivery or return dated before the product was counted is entered after the count. The owner confirms it. See 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off.

Difference, discrepancy

When counted and expected don’t agree: short or over. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Expected

What the ledger says should be in the shop. Counters never see it while counting. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Fingerprint

The code on every page of a count report, made from everything in it. Printing the same count again gives the same code. See 14  Results and the count report.

Item

A word Jholok doesn’t use for a count. Pairs, sets and pieces are always given apart (“18 pairs and 13 pieces”), never added into a number of items. See 1  Stock basics.

Jangad

Stock sent out of the shop on approval, with a memo, for a customer or another jeweller to see. It is still the shop’s stock until it is sold. See 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off.

Karigar

The craftsman who makes or repairs jewellery for the shop. Stock with the karigar is still the shop’s. See 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off.

Lakh (L)

₹1,00,000. See 1  Stock basics.

Ledger

The record of every movement of stock, oldest first. See 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum.

List price

What the shop asks a customer for one piece of a product. See 1  Stock basics.

Making charge

What it costs to make a piece, on top of the metal. Part of a product’s cost. See 1  Stock basics.

Matched

A product whose count agrees with what was expected. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Memo

The numbered slip that goes with stock sent out on jangad. See 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off.

Movement

One change to a product’s stock: opening stock, received, sold, returned, an adjustment or a count adjustment, and a few more. See 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum.

Not a piece

What you choose in a box review when the app outlined something that isn’t jewellery. It is kept, left out, so the app can learn from it. See 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos.

Not in the catalogue

What you choose for a piece in a box whose design has no product. It is left out of the count and listed. See 10  Pieces to identify later.

Odd single

A single earring found without its pair. It is never rounded into a pair: count the whole pairs and add it with Singles in the count sheet. It shows beside the pairs in Review, the result, the report and the CSV, and never changes stock. See 1  Stock basics.

On hand, stock on hand

How many of a product the shop has: the sum of all its movements. See 1  Stock basics and 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum.

Opening stock

The stock a product already had when it was added to Jholok. See 2  The ledger: why stock is a sum.

Order

Stock set aside for a customer’s order. It is not on the shelf, but it is still the shop’s. See 12  Stock off the shelf and the cut-off.

Over

More found than expected. Often a delivery or a return that wasn’t entered. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Owner

The person who runs the shop in Jholok. The owner sets up the people, proves it’s them for exports and backups, and can approve a count. See 4  Setting up the shop.

Pair

Two matching earrings, counted and sold as one. See 1  Stock basics.

Piece

The unit for everything that isn’t earrings or a set: a ring, a chain, a coin. See 1  Stock basics.

Piece tag

A code on one individual piece, different from every other piece’s. It links to its product through the tag list. See 5  The catalogue.

PIN

The short number each person enters to show who they are. An approver’s PIN is their signature on a completed count. See 4  Setting up the shop.

Product

One design in one metal and weight, so that every piece of it is alike. See 1  Stock basics.

Proposal

What a box photo or tag scan finds, before you check it and add it to the count. See 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos.

Reconciliation

Comparing what was counted with what was expected, and explaining every difference. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Recount

Counting a product again. A shortage must be recounted, blind, before it can be accepted. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Review

The screen where an approver sees the counted and expected numbers side by side, and decides which differences to accept. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Separation of duties

Making sure the person who counts isn’t the person who approves, so no one can hide a loss alone. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Set

Pieces sold together as one, such as a necklace with matching earrings. Counted as 1. See 1  Stock basics.

Short

Fewer found than expected. Recounted before it is accepted. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

Shrinkage

Stock lost without being sold: theft, damage or mistakes. See 3  Counting and checking against the ledger.

SKU

Stock keeping unit: a product’s own short code, such as EAR-0002. See 1  Stock basics.

Stock

The jewellery the shop owns and means to sell. See 1  Stock basics.

Stock value

What the stock is worth: each product’s stock on hand times its cost, or its list price, added up. See 1  Stock basics.

Tag list

The list linking each piece tag to its product, imported from a spreadsheet or linked in the app. See 5  The catalogue.

Tag scan

Counting a box by reading each piece’s tag with the camera. Each tag counts its piece once. See 9  Counting boxes: tags and photos.

To identify

The queue of pieces in added box photos that don’t have a product yet. They are identified while the count is open, by whoever is counting, never in Review. See 10  Pieces to identify later.

Type

A group of products, such as Earrings or Rings. A type sets the unit its products are counted in. See 1  Stock basics.

Unit

What a type is counted in: pairs, sets or pieces. Stock is shown in its units, not as one total. See 1  Stock basics.

title: Appendix A — Questions and answers
text:
A.1 Counting
Short answers to the questions people ask most, with the chapter that explains each one.
I tapped + too many times. Tap − to take one off. After a change of more than one, the bar at the bottom offers Undo for a few seconds. Chapter 8
I typed the wrong count. Tap the number again and choose Set total, or swipe left on the product and tap Clear to start again. Chapter 8
The phone rang, or the app closed, in the middle of counting. Nothing is lost: every tap is saved at once. Open the count again from the Count tab. It may ask who’s counting: check that your name is the one chosen. Chapter 8
Why can’t I see how many there should be? Counting is blind on purpose: knowing the answer changes what people find. The approver sees the expected numbers in Review. Chapter 3
I found a single earring without its pair. Count the whole pairs, then add the odd one with Singles on the same sheet. A single is shown beside the pairs and is never rounded into a pair. Chapter 1
A product I’m holding isn’t in the list. Search for it, or use Find by code. If it still isn’t there, it may be a type this count doesn’t cover, an archived product, or a design not yet in the catalogue: tell the owner. Chapter 8
Two of us want to count the same count. Take turns on the shop’s phone. Each time, go back to the counts list, open the count and choose your own name. The count lists you both. Chapter 8
What’s the difference between “None here” and leaving a product blank? “None here” counts 0: you looked and there were none. A product left with a dash wasn’t counted, and keeps its stock unless the approver chooses Set to zero. Chapter 8

title: Appendix A — Questions and answers
text:
A.2 Boxes and tags
The scan says “Product code”. That’s a barcode or SKU, which is on every piece of a design, so it can’t count one piece. Count those pieces on their rows, or with a box photo. Chapter 9
The scan says “Already counted in Box 2”. That piece was counted earlier in this count. It adds nothing, so nothing is counted twice. Chapter 9
The app asks “Is this Box 2 again?” It thinks you may have photographed the same box twice. If you have, tap Cancel. Chapter 9
Picture matches never suggest anything. Picture matching compares pieces with product photos only. Products without a photo, showing a drawing, can’t be matched. Chapter 5
I can’t tell which product a piece in the To identify queue is. Tap See the box to find it in the tray, then look at the piece itself. If it’s a design the shop has no product for, choose Not in the catalogue. Otherwise Skip it and come back. Chapter 10

title: Appendix A — Questions and answers
text:
A.3 Review and completing
A shortage’s tick won’t turn on. It hasn’t been recounted. Tap it under Recount first and count it again. Chapter 13
Complete is greyed out. Some pieces in box photos aren’t identified. Reopen the count so a counter can identify them. Chapter 10
Everyone who approves counted in this count. Then the owner approves it. If the owner counted too, the count says one person counted and approved it. Chapter 4
We need to count some more after submitting. An approver taps Reopen for counting on the count and gives a reason. Chapter 13
The books are older than the counting. Pieces sold in between would look missing. Load newer books, or give the reason and review anyway. Chapter 11

title: Appendix A — Questions and answers
text:
A.4 Stock and the catalogue
A product shows stock below zero. A movement is missing, usually a delivery entered late. Record it with its real date, or count the product. Chapter 2
A product’s stock is wrong, and I know why. Open it, tap Adjust, enter the correct stock and the reason. Adjust waits while the product is being counted. Chapter 6
Can I delete a movement I entered by mistake? No. Put it right with another movement, usually an Adjust with the reason, so the ledger keeps the whole story. Chapter 2
I imported a spreadsheet, but the stock didn’t change. Importing never changes the stock of a product Jholok already has. Count the product instead. Chapter 5
A tag won’t link: it says it’s a product code. A product’s barcode or SKU can’t be a piece tag, because every piece of the design carries it. Use the piece’s own tag. Chapter 5
Pieces are on jangad. Will the count call them missing? No. Pieces sent out in Jholok are off the shelf, and a count doesn’t expect them there. Chapter 12

title: Appendix A — Questions and answers
text:
A.5 Data and privacy
Does Jholok need the internet? No. Everything stays on the phone; nothing is sent to a server or synced. Chapter 15
Can two phones share the shop’s data? No. Jholok keeps the shop on one phone. A backup can move it to another phone, but that replaces what the other phone had. Chapter 15
How often should I back up? After every completed count, and at least once a week. Jholok doesn’t back up by itself. Chapter 15
Why does every export ask for Face ID? A file that leaves the phone can’t be taken back, so the owner confirms each one. Chapter 4
I forgot the owner PIN. On a phone with Face ID, use Face ID, then set a new PIN in Settings → People. On a phone without it, the owner PIN can be reset with the phone’s passcode; the log and the next count’s result say it was reset. Chapter 4
Jholok says it can’t open its data. Nothing has been deleted. Try again, restore a backup, or save the data file so it can be repaired. Chapter 15

title: Appendix A — Questions and answers
text:
A.6 Something went wrong
The app says something “wasn’t saved, so it’s back as it was”. The change didn’t save, often because the phone is nearly full, so Jholok put everything back as it was. Free some space and try again. Chapter 15
The camera says it’s paused. It says why: a call, another app using the camera, the app beside another in Split View, or the phone being too warm. It comes back on its own, or when you open Jholok full screen. Chapter 9
A photo is blurred, too dark or tilted. Tap Retake, or Use anyway if you’re happy with it. Chapter 9
